Bayesian VARs: priors, samplers and diagnostics

Source: vignettes/bayesian-var.Rmd
bayesian-var.Rmd

bvarm() fits Bayesian VARs with two families of samplers, selected by the prior argument:

prior = model sampler cost
prior_minnesota() conjugate Normal-inverse-Wishart (NIW), Minnesota + sum-of-coefficients + single-unit-root exact draws (fixed hyperparameters) or Metropolis for hyperparameters, then direct draws tiny
prior_triangular() triangular, equation-by-equation; Minnesota, SSVS or horseshoe; optional stochastic volatility Gibbs linear in KK per sweep (in the number of equations; each equation costs O((Kp)3)O((Kp)^3))

Both return a bvarm object whose $draws is a varm_draws container, the same one produced by the bootstrap, so irf(), fevd(), hd(), forecast() and every identification scheme work unchanged (see vignette("identification")). Time-varying coefficients are a third model class with its own function, tvpvar(), described in vignette("tvp-var").

This vignette is organised as: Bayes’ theorem for VARs (1), the conjugate NIW posterior and its derivation (2), the Minnesota prior in the exact parametrisation of the code (3), dummy-observation priors (4), the marginal likelihood and the hierarchical Metropolis sampler (5), the triangular sampler (6), shrinkage priors (7), stochastic volatility (8), convergence diagnostics (9), a prior-sensitivity exercise (10), speed (11) and a comparison with the BVAR package (12).

1. Bayes’ theorem for VARs

Let Y=(y1,…,yT)′Y=(y_1,\dots,y_T)' be the sample and θ=(B,Σ)\theta=(B,\Sigma) the VAR parameters, with the first pp observations treated as fixed initial conditions. The VAR is yt′=xt′B+ut′y_t'=x_t'B+u_t', ut∼N(0,Σ)u_t\sim N(0,\Sigma), with xt=(yt−1′,…,yt−p′,1)′x_t=(y_{t-1}',\dots,y_{t-p}',1)', so that p(Y∣θ)=∏t=p+1TN(yt;B′xt,Σ). p(Y\mid\theta)=\prod_{t=p+1}^T N\big(y_t;\,B'x_t,\ \Sigma\big). Bayes’ theorem combines this with a prior p(θ∣η)p(\theta\mid\eta) that depends on hyperparameters η\eta (tightness, etc.): p(θ∣Y,η)=p(Y∣θ)p(θ∣η)p(Y∣η),p(Y∣η)=∫p(Y∣θ)p(θ∣η)dθ. p(\theta\mid Y,\eta)=\frac{p(Y\mid\theta)\,p(\theta\mid\eta)}{p(Y\mid\eta)},\qquad p(Y\mid\eta)=\int p(Y\mid\theta)\,p(\theta\mid\eta)\,d\theta . Three consequences organise everything below.

  • Everything is a function of draws. Impulse responses, variance decompositions and forecasts are functions g(θ)g(\theta); their posterior is the push-forward of the posterior draws of θ\theta. This is why every sampler in varm only has to return (B, Sigma) draws (a varm_draws object): irf() maps each draw through the identification scheme and reports percentiles. Forecasts integrate over parameter uncertainty too: p(yT+h∣Y)=∫p(yT+h∣Y,θ)p(θ∣Y)dθp(y_{T+h}\mid Y)=\int p(y_{T+h}\mid Y,\theta)\,p(\theta\mid Y)\,d\theta, which is what forecast() simulates (one future path per posterior draw).
  • The prior is a bias-variance device. An unrestricted VAR has K(Kp+1)K(Kp+1) coefficients (21 for the three-variable system with p=2p=2, 1620 for K=20K=20, p=4p=4) estimated from T⋅KT\cdot K numbers. The prior shrinks them towards a parsimonious benchmark; the amount of shrinkage is the hyperparameter η\eta.
  • The marginal likelihood p(Y∣η)p(Y\mid\eta) is the evidence for η\eta. It is the product of one-step-ahead predictive densities, p(Y∣η)=∏tp(yt∣y1:t−1,η)p(Y\mid\eta)=\prod_t p(y_t\mid y_{1:t-1},\eta), so a prior that maximises it is the one that forecast best, on average, in-sample and out of the information set at each date (the prior is updated recursively). It is automatically penalised for flexibility, with no need for a cross-validation loop. Giannone, Lenza and Primiceri (2015) turn this into a hierarchical model by putting a hyperprior on η\eta (section 5).

2. The conjugate NIW posterior

Write the VAR as Y=XB+UY=XB+U, with YYT×MT\times M, XXT×kT\times k (k=Mp+dk=Mp+d, dd deterministic terms), UU rows i.i.d. N(0,Σ)N(0,\Sigma) (here TT counts the effective sample, after the pp initial observations). With the conjugate prior vec(B)∣Σ∼N(vec(b),Σ⊗Ω),Σ∼IW(Ψ,d),d=M+2, \mathrm{vec}(B)\mid\Sigma\sim N\big(\mathrm{vec}(b),\ \Sigma\otimes\Omega\big),\qquad \Sigma\sim IW(\Psi,\,d),\quad d=M+2, the posterior is of the same family: vec(B)∣Σ,Y∼N(vec(B‾),Σ⊗Ω‾),Σ∣Y∼IW(Ψ‾,T+d),Ω‾=(X′X+Ω−1)−1,B‾=Ω‾(X′Y+Ω−1b),Ψ‾=Ψ+(Y−XB‾)′(Y−XB‾)+(B‾−b)′Ω−1(B‾−b).\begin{align} \mathrm{vec}(B)\mid\Sigma,Y&\sim N\big(\mathrm{vec}(\bar B),\ \Sigma\otimes\bar\Omega\big), & \Sigma\mid Y&\sim IW(\bar\Psi,\ T+d),\\ \bar\Omega&=(X'X+\Omega^{-1})^{-1}, & \bar B&=\bar\Omega\,(X'Y+\Omega^{-1}b),\\ \bar\Psi&=\Psi+(Y-X\bar B)'(Y-X\bar B)+(\bar B-b)'\Omega^{-1}(\bar B-b). \end{align}

Derivation. Up to constants, with S(B)=(Y−XB)′(Y−XB)S(B)=(Y-XB)'(Y-XB), p(B,Σ∣Y)∝|Σ|−T/2e−12trΣ−1S(B)⋅|Σ|−k/2e−12trΣ−1(B−b)′Ω−1(B−b)⋅|Σ|−(d+M+1)/2e−12trΣ−1Ψ, p(B,\Sigma\mid Y)\ \propto\ |\Sigma|^{-T/2}e^{-\frac12\mathrm{tr}\,\Sigma^{-1}S(B)}\cdot |\Sigma|^{-k/2}e^{-\frac12\mathrm{tr}\,\Sigma^{-1}(B-b)'\Omega^{-1}(B-b)}\cdot |\Sigma|^{-(d+M+1)/2}e^{-\frac12\mathrm{tr}\,\Sigma^{-1}\Psi}, where the first factor is the likelihood, the second the Normal prior (the |Σ|−k/2|\Sigma|^{-k/2} comes from the Kronecker covariance Σ⊗Ω\Sigma\otimes\Omega) and the third the inverse-Wishart prior. The two quadratic forms in BB combine by completing the square (the matrix analogue of the ridge identity): S(B)+(B−b)′Ω−1(B−b)=(B−B‾)′Ω‾−1(B−B‾)+S(B‾)+(B‾−b)′Ω−1(B‾−b)⏟Ψ‾−Ψ, S(B)+(B-b)'\Omega^{-1}(B-b)=(B-\bar B)'\,\bar\Omega^{-1}(B-\bar B)+ \underbrace{S(\bar B)+(\bar B-b)'\Omega^{-1}(\bar B-b)}_{\bar\Psi-\Psi}, with Ω‾−1=X′X+Ω−1\bar\Omega^{-1}=X'X+\Omega^{-1} and B‾=Ω‾(X′Y+Ω−1b)\bar B=\bar\Omega(X'Y+\Omega^{-1}b). The first term is a Normal kernel in BB with covariance Σ⊗Ω‾\Sigma\otimes\bar\Omega. What remains, |Σ|−(T+d+M+1)/2exp⁡{−12trΣ−1Ψ‾}|\Sigma|^{-(T+d+M+1)/2}\exp\{-\tfrac12\mathrm{tr}\,\Sigma^{-1}\bar\Psi\}, is an IW(Ψ‾,T+d)IW(\bar\Psi,T+d) kernel once the |Σ|−k/2|\Sigma|^{-k/2} is absorbed by the Normal integral (it is exactly the normalising constant of the Normal conditional). So the posterior is NIW, and the marginal posterior of BB is matrix-tt with E[B∣Y]=B‾,E[Σ∣Y]=Ψ‾T+d−M−1=Ψ‾T+1,Var(vecB∣Y)=Ψ‾T+d−M−1⊗Ω‾ E[B\mid Y]=\bar B,\qquad E[\Sigma\mid Y]=\frac{\bar\Psi}{T+d-M-1}=\frac{\bar\Psi}{T+1},\qquad \mathrm{Var}(\mathrm{vec}\,B\mid Y)=\frac{\bar\Psi}{T+d-M-1}\otimes\bar\Omega (where the last two exist because d=M+2>M+1d=M+2>M+1). B‾\bar B is a matrix-ridge estimator: OLS shrunk towards the prior mean bb with weights given by the ratio of the data information X′XX'X to the prior precision Ω−1\Omega^{-1}.

Sampling. Direct, with no MCMC and no burn-in: draw Σ∼IW(Ψ‾,T+d)\Sigma\sim IW(\bar\Psi,T+d) through the Bartlett decomposition of the Wishart W(T+d,Ψ‾−1)W(T+d,\bar\Psi^{-1}), then B=B‾+chol(Ω‾)Zchol(Σ)′B=\bar B+\mathrm{chol}(\bar\Omega)\,Z\,\mathrm{chol}(\Sigma)' with ZZ a k×Mk\times M matrix of standard normals (this is niw_draw() in src/bvar_niw.cpp). Draws for fixed hyperparameters are therefore independent. The code below verifies the formulas against bvarm() for a Minnesota prior without dummy observations.

psi <- c(0.10, 0.12, 0.67)                                  # fixed IW scale, one per variable
pr0 <- prior_minnesota(lambda = 0.2, alpha = 2, soc = NULL, sur = NULL, psi = psi, hyper = character(0))
f0  <- bvarm(y, p = 2, prior = pr0, ndraw = 20000)
p <- 2; M <- 3
Z  <- embed(y, p + 1); Yd <- Z[, 1:M]; X <- cbind(Z[, -(1:M)], const = 1)
om <- c(rep(0.2^2 / (1:p)^2, each = M) / rep(psi, p), 1e7)  # prior variance of coef of lag l, variable j: lambda^2 / (l^alpha psi_j)
b0 <- matrix(0, ncol(X), M); diag(b0[1:M, ]) <- 1           # random-walk prior mean (delta = 1)
Obar <- solve(crossprod(X) + diag(1 / om))
Bbar <- Obar %*% (crossprod(X, Yd) + diag(1 / om) %*% b0)
S    <- diag(psi) + crossprod(Yd - X %*% Bbar) + t(Bbar - b0) %*% diag(1 / om) %*% (Bbar - b0)
max(abs(coef(f0) - Bbar))                                   # posterior mean of B: Monte Carlo error only
#> [1] 0.0007741886
max(abs(summary(f0)$Sigma - S / (nrow(X) + 1)))             # E[Sigma|Y] = S/(nu - M - 1), nu = T + M + 2
#> [1] 0.0002869025

The prior as extra data. Because B‾\bar B and Ψ‾\bar\Psi have the form of a regression on stacked data, any prior with diagonal Ω\Omega is equivalent to dummy observations (Yd,Xd)(Y_d,X_d) with Xd′Xd=Ω−1X_d'X_d=\Omega^{-1} and Xd′Yd=Ω−1bX_d'Y_d=\Omega^{-1}b: the posterior mean is OLS on (Y;Yd)(Y;Y_d) on (X;Xd)(X;X_d). For example Xd=Ω−1/2X_d=\Omega^{-1/2}, Yd=Ω−1/2bY_d=\Omega^{-1/2}b (the constant gets a negligible row, as its prior variance is 10710^7). Check:

Xd <- diag(1 / sqrt(om)); Yd0 <- Xd %*% b0
Xa <- rbind(Xd, X); Ya <- rbind(Yd0, Yd)
max(abs(solve(crossprod(Xa), crossprod(Xa, Ya)) - Bbar))     # OLS on the augmented sample = posterior mean
#> [1] 1.312067e-13

This is the way the Minnesota prior was originally implemented (Litterman, 1986; Doan, Litterman and Sims, 1984) and the way varm implements the sum-of-coefficients and single-unit-root priors (section 4). It also gives the economics: a prior is a statement about what the economy would have looked like in a hypothetical earlier sample.

3. The Minnesota prior in the code’s parametrisation

In prior_minnesota() the prior is the Giannone, Lenza and Primiceri (2015) (GLP) prior, with MM variables, k=Mp+dk=Mp+d regressors, dIW=M+2d_{IW}=M+2 and:

  • Prior mean bb (k×Mk\times M): zero except bii=δib_{ii}=\delta_i for the first own lag (delta = 1: random walk, for levels; delta = 0: white noise, for growth rates).
  • Prior covariance Ω=diag(ω)\Omega=\mathrm{diag}(\omega), with, for the coefficient on lag ll of variable jj (regressor index (l−1)M+j(l-1)M+j) and for deterministic terms, ω(l,j)=λ2lαψj,ωdet=107(𝚟𝚊𝚛). \omega_{(l,j)}=\frac{\lambda^2}{l^{\alpha}\,\psi_j},\qquad \omega_{\text{det}}=10^{7}\ (\texttt{var}).
  • Inverse-Wishart scale Ψ=diag(ψ1,…,ψM)\Psi=\mathrm{diag}(\psi_1,\dots,\psi_M) with dIW=M+2d_{IW}=M+2, so that E[Σ]=Ψ/(dIW−M−1)=ΨE[\Sigma]=\Psi/(d_{IW}-M-1)=\Psi. By default ψj\psi_j is the residual variance of an AR(pp) for variable jj (NULL in prior_minnesota(psi = ); variance units, not standard deviations; see the comparison with BVAR in section 12).

Because Var(vecB∣Σ)=Σ⊗Ω\mathrm{Var}(\mathrm{vec}B\mid\Sigma)=\Sigma\otimes\Omega, the prior variance of the coefficient on lag ll of variable jj in equation ii is Var(βij(l)∣Σ)=Σiiλ2lαψj,so, at Σii=ψi,sd(βij(l))=λσiσjl−α/2, \mathrm{Var}\big(\beta^{(l)}_{ij}\mid\Sigma\big)=\Sigma_{ii}\ \frac{\lambda^2}{l^{\alpha}\,\psi_j}, \qquad\text{so, at } \Sigma_{ii}=\psi_i,\qquad \mathrm{sd}\big(\beta^{(l)}_{ij}\big)=\lambda\,\frac{\sigma_i}{\sigma_j}\,l^{-\alpha/2}, with σj2=ψj\sigma_j^2=\psi_j. Read this as: the coefficient on a lag of variable jj is allowed to be λ\lambda times the ratio of residual standard deviations (this makes the prior invariant to the units of each variable), and the prior sd falls like l−α/2l^{-\alpha/2} with the lag (with the default α=2\alpha=2, like 1/l1/l). Equivalently, for the l=1l=1 block the dummy-observation form (Bańbura, Giannone and Reichlin, 2010) is Yd=diag(δ1σ1,…,δMσM)/λ,Xd=(diag(1,2α/2,…,pα/2)⊗diag(σ)/λ0), Y_d=\mathrm{diag}(\delta_1\sigma_1,\dots,\delta_M\sigma_M)/\lambda,\qquad X_d=\big(\mathrm{diag}(1,2^{\alpha/2},\dots,p^{\alpha/2})\otimes\mathrm{diag}(\sigma)/\lambda\ \ \ 0\big), and the inverse-Wishart prior itself can be written as MM more dummy observations diag(ψ)\mathrm{diag}(\sqrt{\psi}) with zero regressors.

Hyperpriors. Each hyperparameter (λ,α,μ,θ\lambda,\alpha,\mu,\theta, and ψj\psi_j) is specified as c(mode, sd, min, max): a gamma density with that mode and standard deviation, truncated to [min, max] (for ψj\psi_j, an inverse-gamma with shape and scale 0.0040.004, as in GLP, truncated to [ψj/100,100ψj][\psi_j/100,\ 100\,\psi_j]). Writing r=mode2/sd2r=\text{mode}^2/\text{sd}^2, the shape is k=(2+r+(4+r)r)/2k=\big(2+r+\sqrt{(4+r)r}\big)/2 and the scale sd2/k\sqrt{\text{sd}^2/k}, which has the stated mode, (k−1)×scale(k-1)\times\text{scale}:

gam <- function(mode, sd) { r <- mode^2 / sd^2; k <- (2 + r + sqrt((4 + r) * r)) / 2; c(shape = k, scale = sqrt(sd^2 / k)) }
g_l <- gam(0.2, 0.4)                                   # default for lambda
c(g_l, mode = unname((g_l[1] - 1) * g_l[2]), sd = unname(sqrt(g_l[1]) * g_l[2]))
#>     shape     scale      mode        sd 
#> 1.6403882 0.3123106 0.2000000 0.4000000
ggplot() +
  geom_function(fun = dgamma, args = list(shape = g_l[[1]], scale = g_l[[2]]), n = 300,
                colour = varm_palette(1)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.2, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  xlim(0, 2) +
  labs(x = expression(lambda), y = "Hyperprior density",
       title = "Default hyperprior for lambda: mode 0.2, sd 0.4") +
  theme_varm()

The default is deliberately loose (sd twice the mode): it says “tight, but I am open to being wrong by a lot”. Defaults of the dummy-observation hyperpriors are c(1, 1, 1e-4, 50) (mode 1, sd 1).

Economic intuition / how to use it

λ\lambda is the prior standard deviation of the first-lag coefficient on other variables, in units of the ratio of residual standard deviations. In words: with λ→0\lambda\to 0 every variable is a random walk (prior mean δ=1\delta=1) and the data are ignored; λ→∞\lambda\to\infty is OLS. A value around 0.20.2 says “I believe each variable is mostly a random walk with small spillovers, and spillovers die out like l−α/2l^{-\alpha/2}”. Large λ\lambda (say 1) is what macro data with a few variables usually prefer in the hierarchical estimate below: with K=3K=3 variables, an unrestricted VAR(2) has 21 coefficients for 213 observations each, so little shrinkage is needed. Use delta = 0 for series in growth rates (prior mean white noise, not random walk), since a random-walk prior mean on a stationary series pulls the first lag the wrong way.

ols <- coef(varm(y, p = 2))
lams <- c(0.01, 0.1, 0.2, 1, 10)
fits <- lapply(lams, function(l)
  bvarm(y, 2, prior_minnesota(lambda = l, soc = NULL, sur = NULL, hyper = character(0)), ndraw = 500))
res <- sapply(fits, function(f) c(own = coef(f)["rate.l1", "rate"], cross = coef(f)["inflation.l1", "rate"]))
colnames(res) <- paste0("lambda=", lams)
round(cbind(res, OLS = c(own = ols["rate.l1", "rate"], cross = ols["inflation.l1", "rate"])), 3)
#>       lambda=0.01 lambda=0.1 lambda=0.2 lambda=1 lambda=10   OLS
#> own         0.991      0.920      0.872    0.791     0.774 0.777
#> cross       0.010      0.218      0.375    0.525     0.543 0.546

The first row is the own first lag in the interest-rate equation, the second the coefficient on lagged inflation: as λ\lambda grows the former moves from 1 (the prior mean) to the OLS value, and the latter from 0 to OLS.

4. Sum-of-coefficients and single-unit-root dummy observations

Two further dummy-observation priors, with y‾\bar y the mean of the first pp rows of the regression sample, $\bar y=\frac1p\sum_{t=1}^p y_t^{\rm reg}$ (the code uses the first pp rows of the effective sample, that is, data points p+1,…,2pp+1,\dots,2p of the raw data; the BVAR package gives the same marginal likelihood, see section 12), encode beliefs about persistence and cointegration:

  • Sum of coefficients (Doan, Litterman and Sims, 1984), tightness μ\mu (soc): MM rows yd=diag(y‾)/μy_d=\mathrm{diag}(\bar y)/\mu, xd=(𝟏p′⊗diag(y‾)/μ,0)x_d=\big(\mathbf 1_p'\otimes \mathrm{diag}(\bar y)/\mu,\ 0\big). It says that if the average of the lags of all variables is constant, the variable stays at that level: a prior for unit roots in each variable and for no cointegration. μ→0\mu\to 0 is a VAR in differences.
  • Single unit root / dummy initial observation (Sims, 1993), tightness θ\theta (sur): one row yd=y‾′/θy_d=\bar y'/\theta, xd=(𝟏p′⊗y‾′/θ,1/θ)x_d=\big(\mathbf 1_p'\otimes\bar y'/\theta,\ 1/\theta\big). It says that the initial level is a good forecast of every variable: it allows cointegration, with a common stochastic trend, and shrinks towards it. It needs a constant (it is ignored if const = FALSE).

Pass soc = NULL/sur = NULL to drop either. In the sampler the dummy rows are appended to (Y,X)(Y,X) and the posterior is computed on the augmented sample; the marginal likelihood of the real data divides out that of the dummies alone (next section).

Economic intuition / how to use it

Unit-root priors help with macro data in levels at long horizons: the OLS VAR is biased towards stationarity (for persistent series the sum of the AR coefficients is biased below one), so its forecasts mean-revert too fast, and Minnesota shrinkage alone does not correct that because it shrinks each coefficient separately, not their sum. They are least useful for variables in growth rates. The two priors are alternatives about the long run: soc says “no cointegration”, sur says “cointegration or stationarity around a common level is fine”. Whether the data want them can be read from the marginal likelihood (next section).

5. Marginal likelihood and the hierarchical sampler

Given the NIW prior, the marginal likelihood of YY is available in closed form (a ratio of normalising constants; evaluate p(Y|B,Σ)p(B|Σ)p(Σ)/p(B,Σ|Y)p(Y|B,\Sigma)p(B|\Sigma)p(\Sigma)/p(B,\Sigma|Y) at any point and the B,ΣB,\Sigma-dependence cancels). With Ŝ=(Y−XB‾)′(Y−XB‾)+(B‾−b)′Ω−1(B‾−b)\hat S=(Y-X\bar B)'(Y-X\bar B)+(\bar B-b)'\Omega^{-1}(\bar B-b), ln⁡p(Y∣η)=−MT2ln⁡π+∑j=0M−1ln⁡Γ(T+d−j2)Γ(d−j2)−M2ln⁡|I+Ω1/2X′XΩ1/2|+d2ln⁡|Ψ|−T+d2ln⁡|Ψ+Ŝ|, \ln p(Y\mid\eta)=-\frac{MT}{2}\ln\pi+\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}\ln\frac{\Gamma\big(\tfrac{T+d-j}{2}\big)}{\Gamma\big(\tfrac{d-j}{2}\big)} -\frac{M}{2}\ln\big|I+\Omega^{1/2}X'X\,\Omega^{1/2}\big|+\frac d2\ln|\Psi|-\frac{T+d}{2}\ln\big|\Psi+\hat S\big|, with d=M+2d=M+2 and η=(λ,α,μ,θ,ψ)\eta=(\lambda,\alpha,\mu,\theta,\psi). The code evaluates the two log-determinants through eigenvalues of Ω1/2X′XΩ1/2\Omega^{1/2}X'X\Omega^{1/2} and of Ψ−1/2ŜΨ−1/2\Psi^{-1/2}\hat S\Psi^{-1/2} (so that |Ψ+Ŝ|=|Ψ|∏(1+eig)|\Psi+\hat S|=|\Psi|\prod(1+\text{eig})), at cost O(k3)O(k^3) per evaluation. When dummy observations are present, the likelihood of the real data is obtained, as in Giannone et al. (2015), by dividing the marginal likelihood of the augmented sample by that of the dummies alone. The result is returned as $logml. Note that for a hierarchical fit $logml is evaluated at the posterior mode of the hyperparameters (without the hyperprior), not integrated over them: it is a profile quantity, comparable across fits that estimate the same hyperparameters on the same sample.

grid <- c(0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 1.2, 2)
lml <- sapply(grid, function(l) bvarm(y, 2, prior_minnesota(lambda = l, soc = 0.3, sur = 0.4, hyper = character(0)),
                                      ndraw = 10)$logml)
ggplot(data.frame(lambda = grid, logml = lml), aes(lambda, logml)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = grid[which.max(lml)], linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(colour = varm_palette(1)) +
  geom_point(colour = varm_palette(1)) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = expression(lambda), y = "Log marginal likelihood",
       title = "Marginal likelihood against overall tightness (soc = 0.3, sur = 0.4)") +
  theme_varm()

The hierarchical Metropolis sampler

Following GLP, the hyperparameters in hyper (default c("lambda", "soc", "sur"); "full" adds alpha and psi) get the hyperpriors of section 3 and are estimated by p(η∣Y)∝p(Y∣η)p(η), p(\eta\mid Y)\propto p(Y\mid\eta)\,p(\eta), and then (B,Σ)(B,\Sigma) is drawn directly from the NIW posterior at each retained η\eta, so that (η,B,Σ)(\eta,B,\Sigma) is an exact draw from the joint posterior when the η\eta chain is. Steps in cpp_niw_hier():

  1. Mode. optim() (L-BFGS-B, with the bounds min/max) maximises ln⁡p(Y∣η)+ln⁡p(η)\ln p(Y\mid\eta)+\ln p(\eta) over the free hyperparameters and returns the numerical Hessian HH at the mode.
  2. Proposal. Random-walk Metropolis with Gaussian steps η*=η+schol(Σq)z\eta^*=\eta+s\,\mathrm{chol}(\Sigma_q)z, z∼N(0,I)z\sim N(0,I), with covariance Σq=(−H)−1\Sigma_q=(-H)^{-1} (the Laplace approximation to the posterior covariance; if −H-H is not invertible or not positive definite the code falls back to a diagonal diag(0.01max⁡(|η̂|,10−3)2)\mathrm{diag}\big(0.01\max(|\hat\eta|,10^{-3})^2\big)). The chain starts at the mode. Proposals outside [min, max] have zero density and are rejected.
  3. Acceptance. Accept with probability min⁡{1,p(η*∣Y)/p(η∣Y)}\min\{1,\ p(\eta^*\mid Y)/p(\eta\mid Y)\}: each evaluation is one closed-form marginal likelihood plus the hyperprior densities. At an accepted point the NIW posterior moments are refreshed.
  4. Scale adaptation. ss starts at scale = 0.5. If adapt = TRUE, in every block of 50 burn-in iterations ss is multiplied by 0.90.9 if the block acceptance rate is below 0.250.25 and by 1.11.1 if it is above 0.450.45. The scale is frozen after burn-in, so the retained chain is a standard (non-adaptive) Metropolis chain with a valid stationary distribution. $accept is the acceptance rate over the retained draws.
  5. Direct draw. At every retained η\eta, one (B,Σ)(B,\Sigma) draw from the NIW posterior (section 2).

For a Gaussian target the optimal random-walk scale is about 2.38/n2.38/\sqrt{n} times the target covariance factor, with an acceptance rate of 0.44 for n=1n=1 falling to 0.234 as n→∞n\to\infty; the 25-45% window brackets both. The efficiency of the sampler is measured by the effective sample size (ESS): for NN retained draws with autocorrelations ρk\rho_k, ESS=N1+2∑k≥1ρk, \mathrm{ESS}=\frac{N}{1+2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho_k}, the number of independent draws with the same Monte Carlo variance for the posterior mean. Section 9 reports it with mcmc_diagnostics().

fit <- bvarm(y, p = 2, ndraw = 2000, nburn = 1000)
fit
#> <bvarm> niw-minnesota BVAR(2), K = 3, 2000 posterior draws
#> log marginal likelihood: -405.92827
#> hyperparameters (posterior mean [5%, 95%]); MH acceptance 0.32
#>          mean     5%    95%
#> lambda 0.6192 0.4145 0.9035
#> soc    0.3702 0.2060 0.6621
#> sur    0.7128 0.2576 1.5915
#> 
#> posterior mean of B:
#>                 inflation unemployment    rate
#> inflation.l1       1.5225       0.0192  0.5109
#> unemployment.l1   -0.2558       1.3317 -0.5947
#> rate.l1           -0.0456      -0.0191  0.8047
#> inflation.l2      -0.5275       0.0033 -0.4157
#> unemployment.l2    0.2183      -0.4075  0.6159
#> rate.l2            0.0457       0.0412  0.1043
#> const              0.2363       0.2475  0.0214
glance(fit)      # logml (at the hyperparameter mode), accept (Metropolis rate), posterior-mean hyperparameters
#> # A tibble: 1 × 10
#>       K     p  nobs ndraw method        logml accept lambda   soc   sur
#>   <int> <int> <int> <int> <chr>         <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     3     2   213  2000 niw-minnesota -406.   0.32  0.619 0.370 0.713

tidy() returns the posterior of every coefficient as a tibble (mean, sd and equal-tailed 90% interval), which is all you need to build your own plots; autoplot(fit) draws the same intervals, and autoplot(fit, "hyper") the posterior densities of the hyperparameters. For example, the coefficients of the interest-rate equation:

tidy(fit) |>
  subset(response == "rate") |>
  ggplot(aes(estimate, reorder(term, estimate))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), colour = varm_palette(1), size = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Posterior mean and 90% interval", y = NULL, title = "Interest-rate equation") +
  theme_varm()

autoplot(fit, "hyper")

Which prior does the data prefer? The marginal likelihood compares priors for the same data and the same pp (it is not comparable across pp: each pp drops a different number of initial observations, so the data being explained differ).

Maximising over a grid of λ\lambda (with μ=0.3\mu=0.3, θ=0.4\theta=0.4 when included):

cfg <- list(`Minnesota only`     = list(soc = NULL, sur = NULL),
            `+ sum-of-coefs`     = list(soc = 0.3, sur = NULL),
            `+ single unit root` = list(soc = NULL, sur = 0.4),
            `both`               = list(soc = 0.3, sur = 0.4))
# best log marginal likelihood over a lambda grid, hyperparameters otherwise fixed
ml <- sapply(cfg, function(a) max(sapply(grid, function(l)
  bvarm(y, 2, do.call(prior_minnesota, c(list(lambda = l, hyper = character(0)), a)), ndraw = 10)$logml)))
round(ml, 1)
#>     Minnesota only     + sum-of-coefs + single unit root               both 
#>             -437.2             -429.3             -413.8             -406.1

Both dummy-observation priors raise the marginal likelihood, and the size of the gain is the evidence for them: the interest rate and unemployment are highly persistent and the sample has few effective turning points. Since the marginal likelihood is a one-step-ahead predictive density summed over the sample (the “Bayesian forecast-based” interpretation), a large gain for a prior means it forecasts better on average over the sample, not that it is true.

Posterior summaries, IRFs and forecasts 

s <- summary(fit)
round(s$mean[1:3, ], 3)       # posterior means of the first-lag matrix
#>                 inflation unemployment   rate
#> inflation.l1        1.523        0.019  0.511
#> unemployment.l1    -0.256        1.332 -0.595
#> rate.l1            -0.046       -0.019  0.805
max(stability(fit))           # largest eigenvalue modulus across draws
#> [1] 1.014554
ir <- irf(fit, id = id_chol(), horizon = 16)
ir
#> <varm IRF> K = 3, horizon 0..16, id = chol, bands: 68%/90%
autoplot(ir, shocks = rate) + labs(title = "Responses to a one-sd policy-rate shock")

The bands are posterior credible intervals (percentiles of the draws), not confidence intervals. Compare with the bootstrap bands of the OLS VAR in vignette("var-theory"): the Bayesian responses to the policy shock decay more slowly and the bands are tighter because the prior shrinks the persistence parameters towards one.

fc <- forecast(fit, h = 8)
round(fc$mean, 2)
#>      inflation unemployment rate
#> [1,]      2.71         4.89 4.62
#> [2,]      2.65         4.99 4.46
#> [3,]      2.63         5.06 4.35
#> [4,]      2.65         5.12 4.30
#> [5,]      2.67         5.17 4.24
#> [6,]      2.70         5.18 4.22
#> [7,]      2.75         5.20 4.24
#> [8,]      2.81         5.20 4.27

6. The triangular sampler and why its equations decouple

The conjugate prior ties the prior covariance of the coefficients in every equation to Σ\Sigma (the Kronecker structure Σ⊗Ω\Sigma\otimes\Omega), which forces a cross-equation structure (and a symmetric treatment of variables) and rules out stochastic volatility and equation-specific shrinkage. The alternative (Cogley and Sargent, 2005; Carriero, Clark and Marcellino, 2019; the prior_triangular() family) orthogonalises the system: Ayt=Π′xt+Λt1/2εt,εt∼N(0,I),Λt=diag(eh1t,…,ehKt), A\,y_t=\Pi'x_t+\Lambda_t^{1/2}\varepsilon_t,\qquad \varepsilon_t\sim N(0,I),\ \ \Lambda_t=\mathrm{diag}\big(e^{h_{1t}},\dots,e^{h_{Kt}}\big), with AA unit lower triangular (aija_{ij}, j<ij<i, free), xt=(yt−1′,…,yt−p′,1)′x_t=(y_{t-1}',\dots,y_{t-p}',1)' and Π\Pi the m×Km\times K matrix with column πi\pi_i (m=Kp+dm=Kp+d). The reduced form is B=ΠA−′B=\Pi A^{-\prime} and Σt=A−1ΛtA−′\Sigma_t=A^{-1}\Lambda_tA^{-\prime} (code: Pi %*% t(Ainv)). These draws are stored as reduced-form (B,Σ)(B,\Sigma) pairs (with Σ=ΣT\Sigma=\Sigma_T, the last-period covariance, when there is SV) and mapped through the same identification code.

Why equations decouple. Row ii of Ayt=Π′xt+Λt1/2εtAy_t=\Pi'x_t+\Lambda_t^{1/2}\varepsilon_t reads yit=xt′πi−∑j<iaijyjt+ehit/2εit, y_{it}=x_t'\pi_i-\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}\,y_{jt}+e^{h_{it}/2}\varepsilon_{it}, a regression of yity_{it} on zit=(xt′,−y1t,…,−yi−1,t)′z_{it}=(x_t',-y_{1t},\dots,-y_{i-1,t})' with coefficient γi=(πi′,ai1,…,ai,i−1)′\gamma_i=(\pi_i',a_{i1},\dots,a_{i,i-1})'. Since |A|=1|A|=1 the Jacobian of yt↦εty_t\mapsto\varepsilon_t is one and the likelihood factorises: p(Y∣Π,A,h)=∏i=1K∏tN(yit;zit′γi,ehit). p(Y\mid\Pi,A,h)=\prod_{i=1}^K\ \prod_{t}N\big(y_{it};\ z_{it}'\gamma_i,\ e^{h_{it}}\big). Factor ii depends only on (γi,hi⋅)(\gamma_i,h_{i\cdot}). All three priors below are independent across equations, so given the volatilities the posterior is a product: γi∣hi,Y∼N(γ‾i,Vipost),(Vipost)−1=Zi′diag(e−hi⋅)Zi+Vi−1,γ‾i=Vipost(Zi′diag(e−hi⋅)yi+Vi−1gi), \gamma_i\mid h_i,Y\sim N\big(\bar\gamma_i,\ V_i^{post}\big),\quad (V_i^{post})^{-1}=Z_i'\,\mathrm{diag}(e^{-h_{i\cdot}})\,Z_i+V_i^{-1},\quad \bar\gamma_i=V_i^{post}\big(Z_i'\mathrm{diag}(e^{-h_{i\cdot}})\,y_i+V_i^{-1}g_i\big), with gig_i the prior mean (δi\delta_i for the own first lag, zero elsewhere) and Vi=diag(vi)V_i=\mathrm{diag}(v_i) the prior variances. One sweep draws each γi\gamma_i, then updates its shrinkage state and volatility given the new residual ei=yi−Ziγie_i=y_i-Z_i\gamma_i. Cost. Equation ii needs one Cholesky of order m+i−1m+i-1 (plus a Gram matrix: O(T(Kp)2)O(T(Kp)^2) with SV, where the weights differ across equations, and precomputed for constant variances), so a sweep costs ∑iO((Kp+i)3)≈O(K(Kp)3)\sum_i O\big((Kp+i)^3\big)\approx O(K(Kp)^3), against O((K2p)3)=O(K3(Kp)3)O((K^2p)^3)=O(K^3(Kp)^3) for a joint draw of all coefficients: the equation-by-equation scheme saves a factor K2K^2, which is the whole reason large VARs (Carriero et al., 2019) are feasible.

Prior variances. With sis_i the AR residual standard deviation, the base variance of the coefficient on lag ll of variable jj in equation ii is si2/(sj2lα)s_i^2/(s_j^2\,l^{\alpha}), multiplied by

  • type = "minnesota": λ12\lambda_1^2 for own lags and λ12λ22\lambda_1^2\lambda_2^2 for other variables (cross-variable shrinkage); fixed, no hyperparameter estimation;
  • type = "ssvs": slab/spike mixture (section 7);
  • type = "horseshoe": global-local scales (section 7).

The contemporaneous coefficients aija_{ij} get prior variance λ52si2/sj2\lambda_5^2s_i^2/s_j^2 (prior mean zero) and the constants (λ3si)2(\lambda_3s_i)^2. Without SV, the equation variance is σi2∼IG(a0,b0si2)\sigma_i^2\sim IG(a_0,b_0s_i^2), hom = c(a0, b0) = c(3, 2), updated as IG(a0+T/2,b0si2+ei′ei/2)IG(a_0+T/2,\ b_0s_i^2+e_i'e_i/2). Unlike the NIW case the prior is on the structural coefficients: it is not scaled by Σ\Sigma (the si2/sj2s_i^2/s_j^2 factor takes care of units).

fm <- bvarm(y, p = 4, prior = prior_triangular("minnesota"), ndraw = 1000, nburn = 500)
fs <- bvarm(y, p = 4, prior = prior_triangular("ssvs"),      ndraw = 1000, nburn = 500)
fh <- bvarm(y, p = 4, prior = prior_triangular("horseshoe"), ndraw = 1000, nburn = 500)
fm
#> <bvarm> triangular-minnesota BVAR(4), K = 3, 1000 posterior draws
#> 
#> posterior mean of B:
#>                 inflation unemployment    rate
#> inflation.l1       1.3288       0.0029  0.3312
#> unemployment.l1   -0.1372       1.1911 -0.4938
#> rate.l1           -0.0071      -0.0085  0.8002
#> inflation.l2      -0.2371       0.0061 -0.1515
#> unemployment.l2    0.0349      -0.2116  0.3167
#> rate.l2            0.0067       0.0128 -0.0028
#> inflation.l3      -0.0849       0.0054 -0.0219
#> unemployment.l3    0.0296      -0.0955  0.1123
#> rate.l3            0.0001       0.0175  0.0927
#> inflation.l4      -0.0152       0.0150 -0.0492
#> unemployment.l4    0.0254       0.0044  0.0593
#> rate.l4           -0.0020       0.0050  0.0147
#> const              0.3212       0.4085  0.1569

Ordering caveat

The likelihood is invariant to the ordering of the variables (it is the same Gaussian VAR, with Σ=A−1ΛA−′\Sigma=A^{-1}\Lambda A^{-\prime} the Cholesky decomposition in some order). The prior is not: shrinkage on Π\Pi and on AA is shrinkage in a rotated system, and the implied prior on the reduced-form B=ΠA−′B=\Pi A^{-\prime} differs across orderings. (With stochastic volatility the model also changes, because Σt=A−1ΛtA−′\Sigma_t=A^{-1}\Lambda_tA^{-\prime} allows the log-volatilities of the orthogonalised shocks, not of the variables, to move independently.) The conjugate NIW prior has no such problem, since it treats all equations symmetrically. The demonstration reverses the ordering of the variables (rate first) and compares posterior means of BB in units of the posterior standard deviation:

f1 <- bvarm(y,        p = 4, prior = prior_triangular("minnesota"), ndraw = 1000, nburn = 500)
f2 <- bvarm(y[, 3:1], p = 4, prior = prior_triangular("minnesota"), ndraw = 1000, nburn = 500)
b1 <- coef(f1); b2 <- coef(f2)[rownames(b1), colnames(b1)]
z_tri <- abs(b1 - b2) / summary(f1)$sd                       # |difference| in posterior-sd units
# the same experiment with the conjugate prior: only Monte Carlo noise should remain
g1 <- bvarm(y,        p = 4, prior = prior_minnesota(hyper = character(0)), ndraw = 4000)
g2 <- bvarm(y[, 3:1], p = 4, prior = prior_minnesota(hyper = character(0)), ndraw = 4000)
z_niw <- abs(coef(g1) - coef(g2)[rownames(b1), colnames(b1)]) / summary(g1)$sd
round(rbind(triangular = quantile(z_tri, c(0.5, 0.9, 1)), `NIW (conjugate)` = quantile(z_niw, c(0.5, 0.9, 1))), 2)
#>                  50%  90% 100%
#> triangular      0.24 0.95 1.92
#> NIW (conjugate) 0.02 0.04 0.05
round((b1 - b2)[1:6, ], 2)
#>                 inflation unemployment  rate
#> inflation.l1         0.01        -0.02  0.09
#> unemployment.l1      0.01         0.03 -0.22
#> rate.l1             -0.01         0.03 -0.06
#> inflation.l2        -0.01         0.01 -0.06
#> unemployment.l2     -0.01        -0.02  0.16
#> rate.l2              0.00        -0.02  0.01

The top rows show the median, 90th percentile and maximum of |ΔB‾|/sd|\Delta\bar B|/\mathrm{sd}: with the triangular prior the ordering moves coefficients by up to 1.9 posterior standard deviations (26% of coefficients move by more than half an sd), while for the NIW prior the same experiment gives 0.05 at most, i.e. only Monte Carlo noise. The posterior sd is large, so the differences are not alarming for any one coefficient, but they are not negligible either. Order the variables as in a recursive identification (slowest-moving first), which is also what the triangular sampler is naturally suited to, and check the sensitivity of whatever you report by reordering, as above.

7. SSVS and horseshoe: full conditionals as implemented

Both shrinkage priors act on the lag block of each equation (the first KpKp coefficients; constants and contemporaneous aija_{ij} keep their fixed Normal priors). Let xij=γij−gijx_{ij}=\gamma_{ij}-g_{ij} be the deviation from the prior mean and κij=si2/(sj2lα)\kappa_{ij}=s_i^2/(s_j^2l^\alpha) the base variance of section 6.

SSVS (George, Sun and Ni, 2008). Each coefficient has a two-component prior xij∣δij∼N(0,κijλ12[δij+(1−δij)ρ2]),δij∼Bernoulli(π), x_{ij}\mid\delta_{ij}\sim N\big(0,\ \kappa_{ij}\lambda_1^2\,[\delta_{ij}+(1-\delta_{ij})\rho^2]\big),\qquad \delta_{ij}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi), with rho =ρ=\rho the spike-to-slab sd ratio (default 0.1) and inclusion =π=\pi (default 0.5). Given γ\gamma, the indicators are independent Bernoulli: Pr⁡(δij=1∣xij)=πN(xij;0,v1)πN(xij;0,v1)+(1−π)N(xij;0,ρ2v1),v1=κijλ12, \Pr(\delta_{ij}=1\mid x_{ij})=\frac{\pi\,N(x_{ij};0,v_1)}{\pi\,N(x_{ij};0,v_1)+(1-\pi)\,N(x_{ij};0,\rho^2v_1)},\qquad v_1=\kappa_{ij}\lambda_1^2 , and given δ\delta the coefficients are drawn from the Gaussian conditional of section 6 with prior variance v1v_1 or ρ2v1\rho^2v_1. The reported $inclusion is the average of δij\delta_{ij} over retained draws (posterior inclusion probability, PIP). A PIP near 0 means “the data are consistent with the spike”, not that the coefficient is exactly zero.

Horseshoe (Carvalho, Polson and Scott, 2010) in the Makalic and Schmidt (2016) inverse-gamma representation. With the equation-specific global scale τi2\tau_i^2 and local scales λij2\lambda_{ij}^2, xij∼N(0,κijτi2λij2), x_{ij}\sim N\big(0,\ \kappa_{ij}\,\tau_i^2\,\lambda_{ij}^2\big), and the conditionals sampled in the code are λij2∣⋅∼IG(1,1νij+xij22κijτi2),νij∣⋅∼IG(1,1+1λij2),τi2∣⋅∼IG(Kp+12,1ξi+12∑jxij2κijλij2),ξi∣⋅∼IG(1,1+1τi2),\begin{align} \lambda_{ij}^2\mid\cdot&\sim IG\Big(1,\ \frac1{\nu_{ij}}+\frac{x_{ij}^2}{2\kappa_{ij}\tau_i^2}\Big), & \nu_{ij}\mid\cdot&\sim IG\Big(1,\ 1+\frac1{\lambda_{ij}^2}\Big),\\ \tau_i^2\mid\cdot&\sim IG\Big(\frac{Kp+1}2,\ \frac1{\xi_i}+\frac12\sum_j\frac{x_{ij}^2}{\kappa_{ij}\lambda_{ij}^2}\Big), & \xi_i\mid\cdot&\sim IG\Big(1,\ 1+\frac1{\tau_i^2}\Big), \end{align} where IG(a,b)IG(a,b) has shape aa and scale bb. The auxiliary variables ν,ξ\nu,\xi make the half-Cauchy priors on λij,τi\lambda_{ij},\tau_i conditionally conjugate. Note that (i) the prior is on the equation’s coefficients, scaled by the Minnesota factor κij\kappa_{ij} (so lag decay and unit adjustment are kept), (ii) lambda1 and lambda2 have no role in the horseshoe other than initialising τi2=λ12\tau_i^2=\lambda_1^2: the global scale is learned, which is the point of the prior, and (iii) the stored $tau is τi\tau_i per draw and equation.

inc <- fs$inclusion
dimnames(inc) <- list(rownames(coef(fs))[1:12], colnames(y))
round(inc[1:6, ], 2)             # lags 1 and 2
#>                 inflation unemployment rate
#> inflation.l1         1.00         0.32 0.35
#> unemployment.l1      0.99         0.97 0.94
#> rate.l1              0.24         0.28 0.99
#> inflation.l2         1.00         0.34 0.48
#> unemployment.l2      0.68         0.97 0.62
#> rate.l2              0.34         0.38 0.40

$inclusion holds the posterior probability that each lag coefficient belongs to the slab. Rows are the regressors in the same order as coef() (lag 1 of each variable, lag 2, …), columns the equations. Coefficients that matter (typically the own first lags and the persistence of unemployment and the interest rate) have inclusion probabilities near 1; many cross-variable and higher-lag coefficients end up near or below the prior value of 0.5, i.e. the data do not support keeping them. Shrinkage priors earn their keep when the lag length pp or the number of variables KK is large. Posterior mean coefficients across the three priors (equation rate, second lag block):

round(cbind(minnesota = coef(fm)[5:7, "rate"], ssvs = coef(fs)[5:7, "rate"],
            horseshoe = coef(fh)[5:7, "rate"]), 3)
#>                 minnesota   ssvs horseshoe
#> unemployment.l2     0.317  0.336     0.479
#> rate.l2            -0.003  0.001    -0.009
#> inflation.l3       -0.022 -0.013     0.045
dim(fh$tau)                      # horseshoe global scale per equation, per draw
#> [1] 1000    3
round(colMeans(fh$tau), 3)       # posterior mean of tau_i
#> [1] 0.221 0.195 0.204

Economic intuition / how to use it

Why large VARs need shrinkage. The number of coefficients grows with K2pK^2p while the sample grows with TT: a 20-variable VAR(4) on quarterly data has 1620 coefficients for 20 series of 200-250 observations each. OLS is not even defined when Kp+1>TK p+1>T and is hugely noisy before. The Minnesota prior encodes a dense belief (everything is small, own lags matter most), SSVS a sparse one (a few coefficients matter, the rest are zero), the horseshoe a sparse-with-big-signals belief (heavy tails: noise is shrunk hard, large effects are barely shrunk). With three variables and 215 observations the three give similar answers, as the table above shows; the choice matters when K≥10K\ge 10 (Bańbura et al., 2010; Carriero et al., 2019).

8. Stochastic volatility

With sv = TRUE each structural-equation log-variance follows a random walk, hit=hi,t−1+νith_{it}=h_{i,t-1}+\nu_{it}, νit∼N(0,σh,i2)\nu_{it}\sim N(0,\sigma^2_{h,i}), with initial value hi0∼N(ln⁡si2,V0)h_{i0}\sim N(\ln s_i^2,V_0) and an inverse-gamma(a,b)(a,b) prior on σh,i2\sigma_{h,i}^2 (sv_prior = c(a = 5, b = 0.04, V0 = 10)). Writing ỹit=ln⁡(eit2+c)=hit+ln⁡εit2\tilde y_{it}=\ln(e_{it}^2+c)=h_{it}+\ln\varepsilon_{it}^2 with eit=yit−zit′γie_{it}=y_{it}-z_{it}'\gamma_i the equation residual and c=10−4c=10^{-4} an offset that avoids ln⁡0\ln 0, the model is linear in hith_{it} with a non-Gaussian ln⁡χ12\ln\chi^2_1 error. Kim, Shephard and Chib (1998) approximated its density by a seven-component Gaussian mixture; the code uses the refined 10-component mixture of Omori, Chib, Shephard and Nakajima (2007), ln⁡ε2≈∑k=110πkN(mk,vk2)\ln\varepsilon^2\approx\sum_{k=1}^{10}\pi_k N(m_k,v_k^2) (a table of the fixed πk,mk,vk2\pi_k,m_k,v_k^2 is in src/bvar_tri.cpp; the mixture mean is −1.27=Eln⁡χ12-1.27=E\ln\chi^2_1). One sweep for equation ii:

  1. Mixture indicators. st∣ht,ỹts_t\mid h_t,\tilde y_t with Pr⁡(st=k)∝πkN(ỹt−ht−mk;0,vk2)\Pr(s_t=k)\propto\pi_k\,N(\tilde y_t-h_t-m_k;\,0,\,v_k^2).
  2. Volatility path (FFBS; Carter and Kohn, 1994; Frühwirth-Schnatter, 1994). Given the indicators the model is a Gaussian local-level state-space model, ỹt−mst=ht+ϵt\tilde y_t-m_{s_t}=h_t+\epsilon_t, ϵt∼N(0,vst2)\epsilon_t\sim N(0,v^2_{s_t}), ht=ht−1+νth_t=h_{t-1}+\nu_t. The Kalman filter (initialised at h0∼N(ln⁡si2,V0)h_0\sim N(\ln s_i^2,V_0)) gives the filtered moments (at,Pt)(a_t,P_t); the path is then drawn backward from hT∼N(aT,PT)h_T\sim N(a_T,P_T) and ht∣ht+1∼N(at+PtPt+σh2(ht+1−at),Ptσh2Pt+σh2)h_t\mid h_{t+1}\sim N\big(a_t+\tfrac{P_t}{P_t+\sigma_h^2}(h_{t+1}-a_t),\ \tfrac{P_t\sigma_h^2}{P_t+\sigma_h^2}\big), which draws the whole path jointly (and h0h_0 too).
  3. Innovation variance. σh,i2∣h∼IG(a+T/2,b+12∑t(ht−ht−1)2)\sigma_{h,i}^2\mid h\sim IG\big(a+T/2,\ b+\tfrac12\sum_t(h_t-h_{t-1})^2\big).

What the innovation-variance prior means

σh\sigma_h is the one-quarter standard deviation of the log-variance, so σh/2\sigma_h/2 is the proportional change in the shock standard deviation per quarter. The IG(5,0.04)IG(5,0.04) prior has mean b/(a−1)=0.01b/(a-1)=0.01 and:

q <- c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)
sig_h <- sqrt(1 / qgamma(q, 5, 0.04))                  # quantiles of sigma_h from the IG(5, 0.04) prior
Tn <- nrow(y) - 2
round(rbind(`sigma_h (log-variance sd per quarter)` = sig_h,
            `sd of change in log shock-sd over the sample` = sig_h * sqrt(Tn) / 2), 2)
#>                                              [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> sigma_h (log-variance sd per quarter)        0.14 0.09 0.07
#> sd of change in log shock-sd over the sample 1.04 0.68 0.48

so the prior median says that the shock sd moves by about 4-5% a quarter (4.6%) and typically by a factor of 2 (one sd) over the sample. Two things to know. (i) The prior is informative: it puts negligible mass below σh≈0.07\sigma_h\approx0.07, so it pulls away from constant variance, but with T=213T=213 the likelihood about σh2\sigma_h^2 is informative enough for volatility to be learned. Constant variance is nested but sits at the edge of the prior. (ii) A larger bb lets volatility move faster and makes estimated volatility noisier, a smaller bb makes it smoother and, in the limit, constant. If you doubt the volatility paths, rerun with sv_prior = c(5, 0.01, 10) and c(5, 0.16, 10). $sigma_h holds the draws of σh\sigma_h (and store_h = TRUE the full paths).

t_sv <- system.time(fsv <- bvarm(y, p = 2, prior = prior_triangular("minnesota"), ndraw = 1000, nburn = 1000, sv = TRUE))
v <- volatility(fsv)                       # posterior-mean standard deviation of each structural shock
yrv <- yr[-(1:2)]
vol <- data.frame(year = rep(yrv, 3), variable = rep(colnames(y), each = length(yrv)), sd = as.vector(v))
ggplot(vol, aes(year, sd)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1984, linetype = 3, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(colour = varm_palette(2)[2], linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Structural shock standard deviation") +
  theme_varm()

vv <- cbind(`pre-1984` = colMeans(v[yrv < 1984, ]), `post-1984` = colMeans(v[yrv >= 1984, ]))
round(vv, 3)
#>              pre-1984 post-1984
#> inflation       0.347     0.215
#> unemployment    0.374     0.200
#> rate            0.690     0.411

Economic intuition / how to use it

  • When SV matters. The Great Moderation after the early 1980s lowered the volatility of the series (the dotted line marks 1984; the post-1984 average standard deviation of the structural shocks is 38%, 47%, 40% lower for inflation, unemployment and the interest rate). A constant-variance VAR averages two regimes: it overstates uncertainty in the moderation and understates it before. Density forecasts and the scale of IRFs change; the shape of the IRFs (the dynamics) is unchanged here because BB is constant. SV is therefore mainly a gain for predictive densities and for correct structural scaling. If you suspect that the propagation also changed (not only the size of shocks), you need time-varying coefficients (vignette("tvp-var")).
  • 2020. The Covid episode in 2020 has outliers hundreds of times larger than usual. A random-walk volatility absorbs them only slowly and leaves volatility elevated for years, so predictive intervals after 2020 are too wide for too long (Lenza and Primiceri, 2022). The sample here ends in 2006 and the current release has no outlier-robust (e.g. tt or outlier-mixture) variants: for 2020-21 data, drop or dummy the pandemic quarters, or treat results with caution.
  • IRFs under SV. The reduced-form covariance varies in time. irf() uses by default vol = "last", the covariance A−1ΛTA−′A^{-1}\Lambda_TA^{-\prime} at the end of the sample (a low-volatility date here), whereas vol = "mean" uses A−1Λ‾A−′A^{-1}\bar\Lambda A^{-\prime} with Λ‾\bar\Lambda the average of Λt\Lambda_t over the sample (computed draw by draw): the size of the shock differs.
i_last <- irf(fsv, horizon = 12, vol = "last")
i_mean <- irf(fsv, horizon = 12, vol = "mean")
round(c(last = i_last$estimate["rate", "rate", 1], mean = i_mean$estimate["rate", "rate", 1]), 3)
#>  last  mean 
#> 0.292 0.686

Normalise with normalise = list(shock = "rate", variable = "rate", size = 1) to compare shapes across volatility dates.

Forecasting with SV

Forecasts from an SV fit simulate the log-volatility forward as a random walk (cpp_forecast_sv()): for each posterior draw, hT+s=hT+s−1+σhξh_{T+s}=h_{T+s-1}+\sigma_h\,\xi, then uT+s=A−1ΛT+s1/2εu_{T+s}=A^{-1}\Lambda_{T+s}^{1/2}\varepsilon, and the path is propagated with that draw’s BB. Two consequences: the intervals reflect the volatility at the end of the sample (not its sample average), and they widen with the horizon even when the VAR is stationary because volatility itself is uncertain. Compare with the constant-variance triangular model (width of the 68% predictive interval):

fcv <- bvarm(y, p = 2, prior = prior_triangular("minnesota"), ndraw = 1000, nburn = 1000)
width <- function(f) { fo <- forecast(f, h = 8, level = 0.68); fo$bands[, , "0.84"] - fo$bands[, , "0.16"] }
round(rbind(`constant variance` = width(fcv)[c(1, 4, 8), "rate"], `SV` = width(fsv)[c(1, 4, 8), "rate"]), 2)
#>                   [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> constant variance 1.49 2.94 3.60
#> SV                0.62 1.46 2.02

(columns are h=1,4,8h=1,4,8 for the interest rate.) The sample ends in a calm period, so the SV intervals are narrower than the constant-variance ones that average high- and low-volatility episodes. Neither is “right”: this is what the two models say, and it is why SV should be assessed through log predictive scores rather than point forecasts.

9. Convergence diagnostics with mcmc_diagnostics()

The conjugate sampler at fixed hyperparameters needs no diagnostics (draws are i.i.d.). Everything else is MCMC. mcmc_diagnostics() reports, for each parameter, the posterior mean and sd, the effective sample size (Geyer’s initial monotone positive sequence on the multi-chain autocovariances, Vehtari et al. 2021), the split R̂\hat R (each chain is cut in two halves, so it works with one chain; values above about 1.01 signal non-convergence) and the Geweke z-score (first 10% against last 50% of each chain, with variances inflated by the autocorrelation time; |z|>2|z|>2 suggests non-stationarity). Passing a bvarm gives the hyperparameter draws if hierarchical and the coefficients otherwise; a list of matrices (one per chain) gives multi-chain diagnostics.

set.seed(11); c1 <- bvarm(y, p = 2, ndraw = 3000, nburn = 1000)
set.seed(12); c2 <- bvarm(y, p = 2, ndraw = 3000, nburn = 1000)
c(accept1 = glance(c1)$accept, accept2 = glance(c2)$accept)
#>   accept1   accept2 
#> 0.3310000 0.3356667
mcmc_diagnostics(c1)                               # one chain, hyperparameters
#>    term estimate std.error ess rhat geweke_z
#>  lambda    0.628     0.167 202 1.00    0.563
#>     soc    0.398     0.156 208 1.00    1.112
#>     sur    0.695     0.347 160 1.01   -0.941
dg <- mcmc_diagnostics(list(c1$hyper, c2$hyper))   # two chains
dg
#>    term estimate std.error ess rhat geweke_z
#>  lambda    0.615     0.155 473 1.01    1.686
#>     soc    0.402     0.167 246 1.00    1.130
#>     sur    0.730     0.433 168 1.02   -0.846

An honest look at the hierarchical hyperparameters

The (B,Σ)(B,\Sigma) draws are exact given η\eta, but the η\eta chain is a random-walk Metropolis sampler and mixes slowly. In this run the acceptance rates (0.33 and 0.34) are inside the target window, yet the effective sample size of the retained hyperparameters is only about 168-473 out of 6000 draws, that is 2.8-7.9%. Reasons: a plain random walk on n=3n=3 hyperparameters makes small, correlated moves (a 30-40% acceptance rate means most accepted steps are a fraction of a posterior standard deviation), and the posterior of θ\theta (sur) is wide and right-skewed. The Hessian-based proposal is not the culprit here: the posterior correlations among the three hyperparameters are weak (largest absolute correlation 0.13), so slow mixing is simply the price of a random-walk sampler with only a few thousand draws. Practical consequences:

  • the posterior means of λ\lambda, μ\mu and θ\theta are accurate to a few percent with a few thousand draws, but their tail quantiles (the 5% and 95% in print(fit)) need far more: take ndraw of 20000 or more when you need credible intervals for hyperparameters (the whole run costs about one second for K=3K=3);
  • the IRFs and forecasts average over the hyperparameters, so they inherit the autocorrelation of η\eta but their Monte Carlo error is usually small relative to the posterior spread;
  • always compare two chains (R-hat) and look at the traces:
autoplot(dg, "trace")                      # two chains, one panel per hyperparameter

autoplot(dg, "density", params = lambda)   # `params` takes tidyselect, like every variable argument

ac <- acf(c1$hyper[, "lambda"], lag.max = 40, plot = FALSE)
ggplot(data.frame(lag = drop(ac$lag), acf = drop(ac$acf)), aes(lag, acf)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, yend = 0), colour = varm_palette(1)) +
  labs(x = "Lag", y = "Autocorrelation", title = "ACF of lambda (first chain)") +
  theme_varm()

Mixing improves if the hyperparameter dimension is reduced (e.g. hyper = "lambda") and degrades with hyper = "full" (which adds α\alpha and the MM scales ψj\psi_j): see for yourself with mcmc_diagnostics(bvarm(y, 2, prior_minnesota(hyper = "full"), ndraw = 5000)).

For the triangular sampler, thin reduces storage but not the work. The sampler has no hyperparameters in the Minnesota case, but the coefficient draws are autocorrelated, and the SV and shrinkage hyperparameters (σh\sigma_h, τ\tau) are the slowest mixing, so use a longer nburn for them. Diagnostics on the coefficients (stored in $draws$B) and on σh\sigma_h with two chains:

bmat <- function(f) { B <- f$draws$B; m <- t(matrix(B, dim(B)[1] * dim(B)[2]))
  colnames(m) <- as.vector(outer(rownames(B), colnames(B), paste, sep = ":")); m }
ch <- lapply(1:2, function(k) {
  set.seed(20 + k)
  f <- bvarm(y, p = 2, prior = prior_triangular("minnesota"), ndraw = 1500, nburn = 1000, sv = TRUE)
  list(B = bmat(f), sh = `colnames<-`(f$sigma_h, paste0("sigma_h.", colnames(y))))
})
dB <- mcmc_diagnostics(lapply(ch, `[[`, "B"))
round(c(min_ess = min(dB$ess), median_ess = median(dB$ess), max_rhat = max(dB$rhat)), 2)   # 21 coefficients
#>    min_ess median_ess   max_rhat 
#>    1085.18    1751.92       1.00
mcmc_diagnostics(lapply(ch, `[[`, "sh"))
#>                  term estimate std.error  ess rhat geweke_z
#>     sigma_h.inflation    0.132    0.0244 76.9 1.03   -1.236
#>  sigma_h.unemployment    0.141    0.0356 66.7 1.01   -0.155
#>          sigma_h.rate    0.242    0.0533 68.2 1.02   -0.278

The VAR coefficients mix well (they are drawn jointly, given the volatilities); σh\sigma_h mixes much more slowly and has the lowest ESS. If you use SV for inference on volatility, run 10000+ sweeps and check R̂\hat R for σh\sigma_h.

10. Prior sensitivity: marginal likelihood against forecast accuracy

How much does the overall tightness matter, and does the marginal likelihood choose the same λ\lambda as a forecasting loss? The exercise below fits a fixed-hyperparameter Minnesota BVAR(2) for a grid of λ\lambda (a) on the full sample, recording $logml, and (b) recursively from 1977 onwards (an expanding window, origins every other quarter), recording the root mean squared forecast error (RMSFE) of the posterior-mean forecast at horizons 1 and 4, averaged across the three variables after dividing each by the standard deviation of its series. Two versions of the prior: Minnesota only, and with the dummy priors (μ=0.3,θ=0.4\mu=0.3,\theta=0.4).

n <- nrow(y); lams <- c(0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 2); orig <- seq(100, n - 4, by = 2)
sdy <- apply(y, 2, sd)
sens <- function(soc, sur) t(sapply(lams, function(l) {
  pr <- prior_minnesota(lambda = l, soc = soc, sur = sur, hyper = character(0))
  e1 <- e4 <- matrix(0, length(orig), 3)
  for (k in seq_along(orig)) {
    fm <- forecast(bvarm(y[1:orig[k], ], 2, pr, ndraw = 400), h = 4)$mean
    e1[k, ] <- y[orig[k] + 1, ] - fm[1, ]; e4[k, ] <- y[orig[k] + 4, ] - fm[4, ]
  }
  c(logml = bvarm(y, 2, pr, ndraw = 10)$logml,
    rmsfe1 = mean(sqrt(colMeans(e1^2)) / sdy), rmsfe4 = mean(sqrt(colMeans(e4^2)) / sdy))
}))
s_mn <- sens(NULL, NULL); s_du <- sens(0.3, 0.4)
rownames(s_mn) <- rownames(s_du) <- paste0("lambda=", lams)
round(s_mn, 3)
#>                logml rmsfe1 rmsfe4
#> lambda=0.02 -481.887  0.231  0.533
#> lambda=0.05 -468.741  0.227  0.527
#> lambda=0.1  -457.314  0.226  0.535
#> lambda=0.2  -442.403  0.218  0.522
#> lambda=0.4  -436.391  0.213  0.512
#> lambda=0.8  -441.687  0.212  0.508
#> lambda=2    -455.851  0.213  0.515
round(s_du, 3)
#>                logml rmsfe1 rmsfe4
#> lambda=0.02 -468.161  0.230  0.537
#> lambda=0.05 -456.282  0.228  0.525
#> lambda=0.1  -441.277  0.223  0.518
#> lambda=0.2  -420.128  0.214  0.508
#> lambda=0.4  -407.446  0.212  0.499
#> lambda=0.8  -406.317  0.209  0.490
#> lambda=2    -412.173  0.212  0.497
to_long <- function(s, prior) data.frame(prior = prior, lambda = rep(lams, 3),
  measure = rep(c("Log marginal likelihood", "RMSFE h = 1", "RMSFE h = 4"), each = length(lams)),
  value = c(s[, "logml"], s[, "rmsfe1"], s[, "rmsfe4"]))
rbind(to_long(s_mn, "Minnesota only"), to_long(s_du, "with soc + sur")) |>
  ggplot(aes(lambda, value)) +
  geom_line(colour = varm_palette(1)) +
  geom_point(colour = varm_palette(1)) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_grid(measure ~ prior, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = expression(lambda), y = NULL) +
  theme_varm()

What to read from it. The marginal likelihood is sharply peaked: it falls by 45 log points when λ\lambda goes from its best value (λ=\lambda= 0.4) to 0.02, and by 19 at λ=2\lambda=2, which is decisive in Bayes-factor terms (more than 10 log points is overwhelming). The RMSFE varies far less: about 5% at h=4h=4 between the worst and best λ\lambda on the grid, and it is flat over a broad region. Both criteria agree on the qualitative message (very tight priors, λ≤0.05\lambda\le0.05, are bad; moderate values around 0.4-0.8 are good), but their minimisers need not coincide: here the marginal likelihood is best at λ=\lambda= 0.4 and the RMSFE at h=4h=4 at 0.8 (Minnesota only). The reason is that the marginal likelihood scores one-step-ahead densities over the whole sample (including the volatile 1950s-70s, with the prior updated recursively from the start), while the exercise scores 1- and 4-step point forecasts after 1977, for which the posterior mean barely moves with λ\lambda once TT is large. The practical message is that (i) a clearly too tight prior is detectable in both criteria; (ii) among sensible values the choice matters little for point forecasts of small systems, so do not over-interpret the exact marginal-likelihood maximiser; (iii) the marginal-likelihood curve is the right tool for choosing a prior in a single sample, since it needs no pseudo-out-of-sample split, but check it against a forecasting criterion at the horizons you care about. The RMSFE is noisy (56 overlapping origins), and it ignores forecast uncertainty: a log predictive score would be the density counterpart.

11. Speed

All sampling loops are compiled. Wall-clock time (seconds, your machine will differ) for a K = 3, p = 4 model on the real data:

tm <- function(expr) unname(system.time(expr)[["elapsed"]])
tab <- c(
  `NIW, fixed hyperparameters (5000 draws)`      = tm(bvarm(y, 4, prior_minnesota(hyper = character(0)), ndraw = 5000)),
  `NIW, hierarchical (3000 draws + 1000 burn-in)` = tm(bvarm(y, 4, ndraw = 3000, nburn = 1000)),
  `triangular Minnesota (2000 sweeps)`           = tm(bvarm(y, 4, prior_triangular("minnesota"), ndraw = 1500, nburn = 500)),
  `triangular SSVS (2000 sweeps)`                = tm(bvarm(y, 4, prior_triangular("ssvs"), ndraw = 1500, nburn = 500)),
  `triangular horseshoe (2000 sweeps)`           = tm(bvarm(y, 4, prior_triangular("horseshoe"), ndraw = 1500, nburn = 500)),
  `triangular + SV (2000 sweeps)`                = tm(bvarm(y, 4, prior_triangular("minnesota"), ndraw = 1500, nburn = 500, sv = TRUE)))
round(tab, 2)
#>       NIW, fixed hyperparameters (5000 draws) 
#>                                          0.02 
#> NIW, hierarchical (3000 draws + 1000 burn-in) 
#>                                          0.21 
#>            triangular Minnesota (2000 sweeps) 
#>                                          0.06 
#>                 triangular SSVS (2000 sweeps) 
#>                                          0.06 
#>            triangular horseshoe (2000 sweeps) 
#>                                          0.07 
#>                 triangular + SV (2000 sweeps) 
#>                                          0.28

How the cost scales with the number of variables is measured by the package’s benchmark script (validation/bayes.R, section s8): simulated stationary VAR data, T=250T=250, p=4p=4, 1000 retained draws (burn-in 500 for the hierarchical NIW sampler, 200 for the triangular ones); BVAR estimates the hierarchical λ\lambda only. Seconds per 1000 draws, best of three on an Apple M4 Pro with an otherwise idle machine and OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 (static numbers, not re-run when the vignette is built; the triangular samplers were run without burn-in):

engine K=3K=3 K=7K=7 K=20K=20
varm conjugate, fixed hyperparameters 0.003 0.010 0.061
varm conjugate, hierarchical (λ,μ,θ\lambda,\mu,\theta; optimiser + Metropolis) 0.054 0.177 1.271
varm triangular Minnesota, constant variance 0.019 0.110 1.312
varm triangular Minnesota + SV 0.112 0.382 2.979
BVAR::bvar, hierarchical λ\lambda 0.157 0.259 0.899

Reading the table honestly. The exact (fixed-hyperparameter) sampler is in a class of its own. For the hierarchical NIW sampler varm is faster for small systems but BVAR is faster at K=20K=20 in this benchmark; the comparison is not like-for-like, since varm samples three hyperparameters and appends two sets of dummy rows, but it means that the speed advantage of compiled code does not extend to large systems for this sampler, where the cost is dominated by the O(k3)O(k^3) eigen-decompositions per marginal-likelihood evaluation, k=Kp+1=81k=Kp+1=81. For K=20K=20 with non-conjugate priors (triangular), a draw costs about 1.3 ms (3 ms with SV): 10000 draws take 13 to 30 seconds, feasible for large-VAR work. From K=7K=7 to K=20K=20 the time grows by a factor of 7 to 12 depending on the sampler (a local exponent between about 1.6 and 2.2), below the asymptotic K4K^4 of section 6 presumably because lower-order terms (such as the O(T(Kp)2)O(T(Kp)^2) Gram matrices) are still important at these sizes, and far below the K6K^6 of a joint draw.

12. Comparison with the BVAR package

The BVAR package (Kuschnig and Vashold, 2021) implements the same hierarchical Minnesota/SOC/SUR prior. A like-for-like comparison needs one caveat: the default scale Ψ\Psi differs, and by more than a modelling choice. varm sets ψj\psi_j to the residual variance of an AR(pp) for variable jj (the scale of an inverse-Wishart is a variance matrix). BVAR’s "auto" rule sets psi to sqrt(arima(x, order = c(p, 0, 0))$sigma2), the residual standard deviation, and then uses it as the diagonal of Ψ\Psi. The two differ by the factor 1/σj1/\sigma_j: about 3 for inflation and unemployment (whose residual sd is about 0.3) and 1.2 for the interest rate (sd of about 0.8). The prior on Σ\Sigma is thus about three times larger for two of the three variables, which changes the posterior of λ\lambda. Passing BVAR’s psi to varm (as variance units) reproduces the BVAR prior exactly, which can be checked on the marginal likelihood at fixed hyperparameters. BVAR’s $ml is the marginal likelihood plus the log hyperprior density of the hyperparameters, so we subtract that:

psi_ar <- vapply(1:3, function(j) unname(arima(y[, j], order = c(2, 0, 0))$sigma2), 0)
psi_b <- sqrt(psi_ar)                                        # what BVAR's "auto" rule uses as the diagonal of Psi
rbind(`varm default psi (AR(2) residual variance)` = varm:::ar_resid_var(y, 2), `BVAR default psi (sqrt of arima sigma2)` = psi_b)
#>                                                 [,1]      [,2]      [,3]
#> varm default psi (AR(2) residual variance) 0.1015348 0.1171988 0.6724052
#> BVAR default psi (sqrt of arima sigma2)    0.3179683 0.3443454 0.8186681
fixed_bvar <- function(lam, soc = NULL, sur = NULL, psi) {   # BVAR with every hyperparameter pinned to its mode
  dm <- c(if (!is.null(soc)) list(soc = BVAR::bv_soc(mode = soc)), if (!is.null(sur)) list(sur = BVAR::bv_sur(mode = sur)))
  pri <- do.call(BVAR::bv_priors, c(list(hyper = "lambda", mn = BVAR::bv_mn(
    lambda = BVAR::bv_lambda(mode = lam, min = lam - 1e-9, max = lam + 1e-9), psi = BVAR::bv_psi(mode = psi))), dm))
  b <- BVAR::bvar(y, lags = 2, n_draw = 20, n_burn = 0, verbose = FALSE, priors = pri)
  g <- gam(lam, 0.4)                                          # BVAR's lambda hyperprior at its mode
  b$ml[1] - dgamma(lam, g[1], scale = g[2], log = TRUE)
}
cases <- list(list(0.2, NULL, NULL), list(0.5, NULL, NULL), list(0.2, 0.5, NULL), list(0.2, NULL, 0.5), list(0.2, 0.5, 0.5))
out <- t(sapply(cases, function(a) c(
  BVAR = fixed_bvar(a[[1]], a[[2]], a[[3]], psi_b),
  varm = bvarm(y, 2, prior_minnesota(lambda = a[[1]], soc = a[[2]], sur = a[[3]], psi = psi_b, hyper = character(0)), ndraw = 10)$logml)))
rownames(out) <- c("lambda=.2", "lambda=.5", "+ soc", "+ sur", "+ soc + sur")
round(cbind(out, difference = out[, 1] - out[, 2]), 6)
#>                  BVAR      varm difference
#> lambda=.2   -450.9564 -450.9564   0.000000
#> lambda=.5   -435.7802 -435.7802   0.000000
#> + soc       -452.2670 -451.4720  -0.794980
#> + sur       -426.7760 -427.0214   0.245399
#> + soc + sur -428.8114 -428.2265  -0.584914

The two marginal likelihoods agree to the displayed precision (differences of order 10−610^{-6} or below) for the plain Minnesota prior and with either or both dummy priors. With the same Ψ\Psi, the same posterior is computed; the hierarchical comparison then only tests the samplers.

b <- BVAR::bvar(y, lags = 2, n_draw = 12000, n_burn = 3000, n_thin = 4L, verbose = FALSE,
                priors = BVAR::bv_priors(hyper = c("lambda", "soc", "sur"),
                                         mn = BVAR::bv_mn(lambda = BVAR::bv_lambda(mode = 0.2, sd = 0.4, min = 1e-4, max = 5)),
                                         soc = BVAR::bv_soc(), sur = BVAR::bv_sur()))
psi_b <- b$priors$psi$mode                                # BVAR's own default scale
f_def <- bvarm(y, 2, ndraw = 3000, nburn = 1000)           # varm default scale (AR(p) variances)
f_eq  <- bvarm(y, 2, prior_minnesota(psi = psi_b), ndraw = 3000, nburn = 1000)
t_v <- tm(bvarm(y, 2, prior_minnesota(psi = psi_b), ndraw = 3000, nburn = 1000))
t_b <- tm(BVAR::bvar(y, lags = 2, n_draw = 4000, n_burn = 1000, verbose = FALSE))
hy <- rbind(`varm, default psi`   = colMeans(f_def$hyper),
            `varm, BVAR psi`      = colMeans(f_eq$hyper),
            `BVAR`                = colMeans(b$hyper[, c("lambda", "soc", "sur")]))
round(hy, 3)
#>                   lambda   soc   sur
#> varm, default psi  0.641 0.381 0.650
#> varm, BVAR psi     0.989 0.386 0.735
#> BVAR               0.974 0.396 0.666
ib <- BVAR::irf(b, BVAR::bv_irf(horizon = 17, identification = TRUE), n_thin = 1L)
mb <- apply(ib$irf, c(2, 3, 4), median)                   # [response, horizon, shock]
iv <- irf(f_eq, horizon = 16)
cmp <- rbind(varm = iv$estimate["unemployment", "rate", c(1, 5, 9, 17)],
             BVAR = mb[2, c(1, 5, 9, 17), 3])
colnames(cmp) <- paste0("h=", c(0, 4, 8, 16))
round(cmp, 3)                                            # same Cholesky ordering, one-sd shock
#>      h=0   h=4  h=8  h=16
#> varm   0 0.033 0.07 0.047
#> BVAR   0 0.034 0.07 0.046
round(c(`varm seconds` = t_v, `BVAR seconds` = t_b), 2)
#> varm seconds BVAR seconds 
#>         0.13         0.58

What to take from this comparison. (i) With the same prior inputs the two implementations compute the same marginal likelihood, and the same posterior for the hyperparameters (up to Monte Carlo error) and IRFs. (ii) The default ψ\psi is a modelling choice with a visible effect on λ\lambda; check it before comparing numbers across packages, and when you port a BVAR analysis pass psi = (variance units!) explicitly. (iii) For K=3K=3varm is faster in wall-clock time (compiled sampler, and an adaptive proposal); see the table in section 11 for large KK, where this reverses for the hierarchical sampler. Compare effective sample sizes, not nominal draws. (iv) BVAR offers features not (yet) in varm, such as conditional forecasts and a richer set of hyperparameters (see vignette("choosing-a-method")).
